1:
No one here is confident about the country. Adam Clarke calls this one of the most obscure prophecies in the book, its subject, design, audience, occasion and both parties to the embassy all doubtful, though he supposes Egypt. John Gill lists candidates without choosing: Assyria, whose outstretched wings closed the preceding chapter; Judea, sheltering under others' wings; and, as the more received sense, Egypt or Ethiopia. John Calvin cannot determine it either, but rules out Egypt as a whole, since the next chapter treats Egypt separately, and rules out the Troglodytes, who by the old geographers had no intercourse with other nations and screeched like bats rather than spoke. John Wesley leaves it at Ethiopia beyond Egypt, or Egypt.

Two do decide. Keil and Delitzsch say flatly that it is Ethiopia, against the expositors who make the strangely described people Israel, and hold that the prophecy predicts the destruction of Sennacherib's army, the expedition being still impending and the envoys carrying urgent commands to their own people, not seeking help from Judah. Charles Ellicott names Tirhakah, whose movements from the upper Nile, subduing Egypt and preparing to meet the Assyrian, had raised the hopes of Hezekiah's counsellors who trusted in an arm of flesh, and to whom the prophet turns with warning; the phrase about the river he takes for the region of the White and Blue Nile. Matthew Henry, weighing Egypt against an Ethiopia he places east of Canaan rather than in Africa, has Tirhakah offering the Jews the shadow of his wings by a diversion against Assyria, and God slighting the offer and taking his own course to protect Jerusalem.

The wings themselves are read four ways. Gill rejects birds flocking to a hot country and proposes the mountains that encompass part of Ethiopia, or the sails of ships. Wesley collects the scriptural uses of the word for battlements, an army and a ship's sails, and makes the land overspread with armies or ships. Ellicott lists an imperial eagle, the winged disk that appears in Egyptian painting as the emblem of Ethiopian sovereignty, and a rendering of resounding instead of shadowing pointing to the swarms of biting fly; he prefers the disk, confirming it from an inscription in which chiefs cry to an Ethiopian conqueror, grant us to be under thy shadow. Clarke takes the phrase for a musical instrument altogether, the winged cymbal, since the Hebrews had no name for the Egyptian sistrum, not using one.

On the boats there is agreement and a reason for it. Clarke notes that vessels of papyrus suit Egypt exactly, quoting two Latin authors for weaving ships from the plant. Calvin supplies the cause: the Nile channel is dangerous at the cataracts, so wooden ships would be dashed on the rocks and pliant materials are necessary. Wesley adds that reed boats were cheaper, swifter and light enough to carry overland. Gill, taking the word for ambassadors in its other sense of images, passes on the conjecture that the vessels carried the head of one Egyptian god and the image of another.

The description of the nation divides translators from expositors. Ellicott would drop the supplied word of saying, making the clause the prophet's own charge to the messengers as he sends them home, and would render the pair of terms tall and polished rather than scattered and peeled; a nation of command rather than meted out and trodden down; and rivers that fertilise rather than spoil. Clarke keeps closer to the received words but renders the first stretched out in length, Egypt being one long vale with the river down its middle, and takes the swift messengers for no particular persons but the ordinary carriers of news. Wesley reads scattered of a people dwelling apart rather than banished, which suits Ethiopian habits, and peeled of hair plucked off, a figure of calamity signifying their approaching ruin.
3:
The summons to the world is a call for witnesses; the disagreement is over who raises the signal. Adam Clarke makes God the agent and takes the standard and trumpet for the meteors themselves, the thunder, lightning, storm and tempest accompanying the Assyrian army's destruction, calling this a bold metaphor and comparing the Greek poet who has the wide earth crash and the great heaven sound like a trumpet as the gods go to battle. Charles Ellicott leaves the agent out, rendering both clauses indefinitely, when an ensign is set up and a trumpet sounded, and hears the prophet calling every nation, Ethiopia included, to watch for a signal as distinct as a beacon-fire on a hill or the alarm of a trumpet, proclaiming the downfall of Assyria. John Wesley has God gathering the nations by ensign and trumpet to execute his judgments. John Gill offers two readings: the prophet summons the world to be eye and ear witnesses of a judgment so manifest that all shall see it, or the messengers address the doomed nation, assuring them that however secure they are they will soon see the sign and hear the alarm.

John Calvin adds a point of tense. The verbs are future, and though some render them as imperatives after the custom of Scripture, he thinks the future better: the most distant nations will be witnesses, because the war originated not with men but with God, who will prove himself its author by remarkable tokens. When wars are waged, he observes, everyone sees plainly what is done, but most men ascribe their beginning and end to chance.

The divine rest that follows is taken as the withholding of help. Wesley explains that God is said in Scripture to rest when he does not act on a people's behalf, and reads the clear heat and the dew-cloud as influences that scorch the herbs and come unwelcome in harvest. Clarke states the argument of the rest of the chapter: God would comfort his own people though they were threatened with immediate destruction, the great designs of the Assyrian would be frustrated and his expectations rendered abortive just as he thought them ripe, the chief part of his army made a prey for beasts and fowls, and Egypt, delivered and avenged, would give thanks. Calvin prefers to read the connecting particle as for rather than and, the prophet answering a doubt that would otherwise perplex weak minds; when confusion arises there is a veil concealing the providence of God.

The vine of the fifth verse draws a correction from Clarke and a moral from Calvin. Clarke observes that the word is the vine's blossom, the vine being understood, and that a defective pointing has led many interpreters, our translators among them, into a grievous mistake, taking that word for the predicate when it is the subject; for how, he asks, can the swelling grape become a blossom? Calvin renders the opening literally as in presence of the harvest, and finds his standing lesson in it: the wicked are not cut off at once but flourish and are spared, until at the moment the fruit is expected they are stripped of it and rooted out with their offspring. Gill carries the metaphor over to the schemers, whose designs are cut short before they are ripe for execution, though they had promised themselves a large harvest of their neighbours. Wesley times it at the moment the bud has turned into a grape and gives hope of a good vintage, and puts the reversal shortly: instead of gathering the grapes he cuts down the tree. Keil and Delitzsch print these verses with the next two and pick their comment up only at the last of them, asking what effect the act of God described here would have on the Ethiopian kingdom if it should now take place.
6:
What the unripe fruit stands for comes first. Charles Ellicott says figure and reality are strangely blended, the grapes cut off being the carcases of the Assyrian host left unburied for the vultures. John Gill allows that reading, and also the destruction of Ethiopians or Egyptians whose princes and people would fall together unburied. John Calvin generalises: they are cast aside as worthless, like the chaff on the dunghill in the Baptist's preaching, and men who thought themselves safe are thrown down beneath all men and the beasts. John Wesley keeps to the branches cut down and left with the unripe grapes on them, so birds and beasts may shelter or feed there all year.

Who brings the present of the closing verse, and who is presented, divides them sharply. Ellicott takes the people to be themselves the gift, reading a people rather than of the people, and has the nation the prophet keeps describing instead of naming offer itself to God's service; he finds the parallel in the psalm where Ethiopia stretches out her hands to God, and thinks the messengers who justified the prophet's words were perhaps among the envoys who later carried gifts to Jerusalem. Adam Clarke keeps givers and gift apart. The Egyptians were in alliance with Judah and fellow-sufferers under the same invader, and so nearly interested in its deliverance; when many afterwards brought gifts to Jerusalem and presents to Hezekiah, he does not doubt the Egyptians distinguished themselves.

Clarke then makes the textual point that decides how much the verse can carry. Instead of a people the Greek and Latin read from a people, which the repetition in the next line confirms, and the difference matters: on that reading the prediction of Egypt's admission into the true Church is not so explicit here as it might seem, though the event is clearly foretold at the end of the following chapter.

Calvin reads the same preposition to the opposite effect, applying the verse to the Jews. He points back to the second verse, where the same descriptions were used of the Jewish people, and takes from a people to mean it will not be an entire nation: though reduced to a feeble remnant, those few left will be offered in sacrifice to God. He draws the lesson for his own day, when the Church seemed to him plundered and trodden under foot: to whatever extent the body is torn into fragments, God will unite the members by his Spirit and never let the calling on his name perish, and those he joins in one spirit he can collect into one body however widely separated.

The rest of his comment turns on how worship is described. The prophets speak of it by outward acts, because worship is within the soul and can be set out only by signs in which men declare that they adore God; the mountain is named because the word went out from it, so it stands for pure and uncorrupted worship. From this he infers that there is no other way of belonging to the Church than by being offered to God in sacrifice, so whoever wishes to belong to him should present himself as an oblation and live no longer to himself. It is not necessary, he adds, to run to Jerusalem, since Zion is now as wide as the world; what is needed is that the same faith dwell in us and that we be joined by the bond of love, without which all about us is heathen.

Gill and Wesley agree on the timing and leave the identification alone. Gill says the present is brought not when the destruction falls but some time after, in gospel times. Wesley puts it at or after that time, when the judgment has been fully executed, and has the people spoken of present themselves and their sacrifices to the true God.
